title: L-Cysteine for Hangovers: What the Finnish Trial Really Found
excerpt: Does L-cysteine help hangovers? An honest look at the 2020 Finnish trial behind the claims, how L-cysteine relates to NAC, the studied dose, timing, and safety.
metaDescription: Does L-cysteine help hangovers? What the 2020 Finnish trial found, its limits, how it compares to NAC, the studied 1,200 mg dose, timing, and safety.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** L-cysteine is one of the few hangover supplements with a real human trial behind it, but that trial was small. A 2020 randomized, placebo-controlled study from Finland, published in *Alcohol and Alcoholism*, found that people who took L-cysteine (1,200 mg in total) around a heavy drinking session reported less nausea and headache the next day, and a lower dose was linked to less stress and anxiety. That's encouraging. It's also one study, in fewer than twenty young men, testing a tablet that also contained vitamins. It hasn't been repeated by an independent team. L-cysteine is a reasonable thing to be curious about, not a proven hangover cure.

**The quick take:** If you want to try it, the dose that was studied was 1,200 mg spread across the drinking session, not a single pill the next morning. It's an amino acid your body already uses, and it's generally well tolerated at those amounts for healthy adults, but it doesn't stop you from getting drunk, doesn't protect your liver from heavy drinking, and won't fix a hangover caused by drinking far more than your body can handle. NAC (N-acetylcysteine) is a close relative, and we explain below how the two differ.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article summarizes published research for general information. It is not a substitute for advice from a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history. **Talk to a doctor before taking L-cysteine or NAC if** you are pregnant or breastfeeding, have kidney disease or a history of kidney stones (especially cystinuria), have asthma, take nitroglycerin or other heart medicines, take blood thinners, or take any prescription medication regularly. If you drink heavily most days, the most useful conversation to have is about the drinking itself, not supplements. In an emergency, such as someone who is unresponsive, vomiting while barely conscious, or breathing slowly after drinking, call 911.

## What L-Cysteine Is

L-cysteine is an amino acid, one of the building blocks of protein. You eat it every day in foods like eggs, poultry, dairy, legumes, and whole grains, and your body can also make it from another amino acid, methionine. It's classed as "conditionally essential," which means most healthy people make enough, but needs can go up during illness or stress.

What makes cysteine chemically interesting is a sulfur group on its side chain, called a **thiol**. Thiols are reactive. They can grab onto other molecules and neutralize them. That single property explains almost everything people hope L-cysteine will do after drinking:

- **It's the limiting ingredient in glutathione.** Glutathione is your body's main internal antioxidant, made from three amino acids: cysteine, glutamate, and glycine. Of the three, cysteine is usually in shortest supply, so how much cysteine you have sets how fast you can make glutathione. We cover glutathione in its own article on [glutathione for hangovers](/never-hungover/glutathione-for-hangover).
- **It can bind acetaldehyde directly.** Acetaldehyde is the toxic chemical your liver makes when it first breaks down alcohol. Cysteine's thiol group can react with acetaldehyde and form a stable, harmless compound. This is the main reason researchers got interested in cysteine for hangovers in the first place.

You'll see L-cysteine sold on its own, inside "hangover" blends, and in a few DHM formulas. Don't confuse it with **L-cystine** (with an "i"), which is two cysteine molecules joined together and behaves differently in the body.

## Why Acetaldehyde Matters for Hangovers

To see why cysteine might help, it helps to know what alcohol does after you swallow it.

Your liver handles alcohol in two main steps:

1. An enzyme called **alcohol dehydrogenase** turns alcohol (ethanol) into **acetaldehyde**.
2. A second enzyme, **aldehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH)**, turns acetaldehyde into acetate, which is relatively harmless and eventually becomes carbon dioxide and water.

Acetaldehyde is the nasty middle step. It's toxic, it irritates tissues, and it's linked to the flushing, nausea, racing heart, and headache that some people get when they drink. People who carry a common genetic variant that slows ALDH (frequent in East Asian populations) build up more acetaldehyde and often get these symptoms strongly after just a drink or two.

Whether acetaldehyde is the main cause of an ordinary hangover the next morning is still debated. By the time a hangover peaks, most alcohol and acetaldehyde have usually cleared from the blood. Researchers now think hangovers come from several things at once: the immune system's inflammatory response, disrupted sleep, mild dehydration, low blood sugar, irritation of the stomach lining, and lingering effects of acetaldehyde and other by-products. So even a supplement that does a good job on acetaldehyde would only be hitting part of the problem.

### The early animal research

The idea that cysteine might soak up acetaldehyde goes back decades. In 1974, a research group led by Herbert Sprince reported in the journal *Agents and Actions* that giving rats L-cysteine (along with thiamine) protected them from a dose of acetaldehyde that would otherwise have been lethal. That study used enormous doses of acetaldehyde in animals, which is nothing like a night out in a person. But it established the basic chemistry and inspired later human work.

## The 2020 Finnish L-Cysteine Hangover Trial

This is the study that most L-cysteine hangover claims trace back to, so it's worth understanding in detail, including what it can and can't tell you.

**The paper:** "L-Cysteine Containing Vitamin Supplement Which Prevents or Alleviates Alcohol-related Hangover Symptoms: Nausea, Headache, Stress and Anxiety," published in *Alcohol and Alcoholism* in 2020. The research was led by C. J. Peter Eriksson, a long-time alcohol researcher at the University of Helsinki, with colleagues in Finland.

### How the study worked

- **Participants:** 19 healthy young men.
- **Design:** randomized, double-blind, and placebo-controlled, using a crossover setup. That means each man took part in more than one drinking session, once with L-cysteine and once with a placebo, and neither the participants nor the researchers knew which was which at the time. Each person acted as his own comparison, which helps a small study detect differences.
- **The alcohol:** a heavy dose, scaled to body weight and drunk over a few hours. This was a deliberate, real hangover-inducing amount, not one or two drinks.
- **The supplement:** tablets containing L-cysteine plus vitamins (B vitamins and vitamin C were part of the formula). The tablets were taken spread out over the drinking session rather than all at once. The total L-cysteine dose was **1,200 mg** in the main comparison, and a **600 mg** total was also tested.
- **What they measured:** next-day hangover symptoms rated by the participants, including nausea, headache, stress, and anxiety, and the participants' desire to drink alcohol again the following day.

### What it found

- At the **1,200 mg** dose, participants reported **less nausea and less headache** the next day compared with placebo.
- At the **600 mg** dose, the clearer effects were on **stress and anxiety**, the anxious, on-edge feeling sometimes called "hangxiety."
- The authors also reported a reduced **desire to drink** the next day in some analyses, which they suggested could matter for people at risk of repeated heavy drinking.

The researchers concluded that L-cysteine may be useful for preventing or easing hangover symptoms and called for larger studies.

### The limitations, stated plainly

A fair reading of this study has to include its weaknesses. None of these make the result wrong. They make it uncertain.

1. **It was small.** Nineteen people is enough to see a signal but not enough to know how big the effect really is or who it works for. Small studies are prone to results that shrink or disappear when someone repeats them with more people.
2. **Only young, healthy men.** We don't know how well the results apply to women, older adults, people who drink regularly, or people with health conditions. Women generally reach higher blood alcohol levels on the same dose per body weight, and that could change the picture.
3. **The tablet wasn't pure L-cysteine.** Because the formula included vitamins, you can't be fully sure how much of the effect came from cysteine alone. The authors argued cysteine was the active ingredient, which is plausible, but the design doesn't prove it.
4. **Some results were mixed across doses.** One dose helped some symptoms and the other dose helped others. That's not unusual in small trials, but it's a reason to be careful with neat headlines like "L-cysteine cuts hangovers in half."
5. **Self-reported symptoms.** Hangover severity was rated by the participants. That's standard in hangover research, because there's no blood test for a hangover, but it adds noise.
6. **No independent replication yet.** As far as we know, no separate research group has repeated the trial. Until someone does, it's one encouraging data point. It's also worth knowing that products built around cysteine-based hangover formulas have been sold commercially, and readers can check the paper's own funding and conflict-of-interest statements. Industry links are common in supplement research and don't make a study wrong, but they're a reason to want independent confirmation.

### So what does it actually tell us?

It tells us that L-cysteine, taken during heavy drinking at around 1,200 mg in total, *may* reduce some next-day symptoms in healthy young men, with nausea and headache the most consistent results. It does not tell us that L-cysteine works for everyone, that it reduces liver damage, or that it lets you drink more safely. For context on how this compares to the evidence for other ingredients, see our [guide to hangover supplements that actually work](/never-hungover/hangover-supplements-complete-guide-what-actually-works-2025).

## L-Cysteine vs. NAC: How They're Related

You'll often see L-cysteine and NAC mentioned together, and for good reason. **NAC (N-acetylcysteine)** is simply cysteine with an extra small chemical group (an acetyl group) attached. Once it's in the body, NAC is converted back into cysteine. So in a sense, NAC is a delivery form of cysteine.

The two aren't interchangeable, though. Here's how they compare in practice:

| | L-cysteine | NAC (N-acetylcysteine) |
|---|---|---|
| What it is | The amino acid itself | Cysteine with an acetyl group attached; converted to cysteine in the body |
| Hangover evidence | One small 2020 randomized trial (positive for nausea, headache, anxiety) | One small 2021 randomized trial with no clear overall benefit; a possible effect in women needing confirmation |
| Main medical use | Mostly a food and supplement ingredient | Hospital antidote for acetaminophen (Tylenol) overdose; also used to thin mucus |
| Stability | Can oxidize in the gut and in storage; less is thought to reach cells intact | More stable and widely studied in medicine |
| Regulatory status (US) | Sold as a dietary supplement | Approved drug ingredient; its supplement status was questioned by the FDA in recent years, though it remains widely sold |
| Typical side effects | Stomach upset, nausea at higher doses | Stomach upset, nausea, unpleasant sulfur smell; rare allergic-type reactions with IV use |

### The NAC hangover trial

NAC got its own hangover test in a randomized, placebo-controlled trial published in *Scientific Reports* in 2021. Volunteers took NAC or a placebo around a drinking session and rated their hangovers the next day. Overall, NAC didn't produce a clear benefit. The researchers noted a possible effect in women, but the study wasn't large enough to be confident about that, and it needs to be repeated.

So, oddly, the plain amino acid has the more encouraging hangover result, even though NAC is the better-studied compound overall. That could mean timing and formulation matter, or it could just reflect how noisy small studies are. Two small trials pointing in somewhat different directions is exactly the situation where you shouldn't treat either result as settled.

### Why NAC's hospital use doesn't mean it cures hangovers

NAC is famous as the antidote to acetaminophen overdose. In that setting, it refills the liver's glutathione so it can neutralize a toxic by-product of acetaminophen. People sometimes jump from there to "NAC protects the liver from alcohol, so it must stop hangovers." That's a leap. The hospital use involves very large IV or oral doses given under medical supervision for a specific poisoning. It doesn't tell us much about a 600 mg capsule taken with a few cocktails. And a daily NAC pill is never a substitute for emergency care after a possible acetaminophen overdose. If that's on your mind, our article on [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) covers the warning signs.

For a fuller comparison of NAC with DHM, including the liver research, see our [NAC vs. DHM guide](/never-hungover/nac-vs-dhm-which-antioxidant-better-liver-protection-2025).

## L-Cysteine Dosage for Hangovers

There's no official dose of L-cysteine for hangovers, because it isn't an approved hangover treatment. The only human hangover data we have come from the Finnish study, so that's the most defensible reference point:

- **Total studied dose:** 1,200 mg, split across the drinking session. A 600 mg total was also tested.
- **Timing:** taken *during* drinking, not just the next morning. The thinking is that cysteine needs to be present while acetaldehyde is being produced.
- **With food and water:** as with most supplements, taking it with food may reduce stomach upset. Food also slows alcohol absorption, which helps on its own.

A few cautions:

- **More isn't better.** We have no evidence that doses above 1,200 mg help hangovers more, and very high doses of cysteine aren't well studied for safety.
- **Check what's already in your product.** Many hangover blends include some L-cysteine, often 100 to 600 mg per serving. If you add standalone L-cysteine on top, count the total.
- **A morning-after dose is untested.** If you take L-cysteine only once you already feel awful, you're outside what the study looked at. It may do little at that point.

### Can you take L-cysteine with DHM?

Yes, there's no known harmful interaction between the two, and some products combine them. They're thought to work in different ways. DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound that has been studied mainly in animals for its effects on alcohol metabolism and on GABA receptors in the brain, while cysteine is aimed at acetaldehyde and glutathione. Neither has strong large-scale human evidence for hangovers, so combining them is reasonable but not proven to be better than either alone.

If you want a product that already pairs them, [No Days Wasted DHM Detox](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) lists L-cysteine alongside 1,000 mg of DHM, milk thistle, and B vitamins. Its per-serving L-cysteine amount is lower than the total studied in the Finnish trial, so it isn't a copy of that study's formula. If you'd rather keep things separate and control each dose yourself, a plain DHM option such as [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20) can be paired with a standalone L-cysteine supplement. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers DHM timing and amounts.

## Safety and Side Effects

At the amounts used in hangover research, L-cysteine is generally well tolerated by healthy adults. It's a normal part of the diet, and the body has well-worn pathways for handling it. That said, "natural" doesn't mean risk-free.

**Common side effects** are mostly digestive: nausea, stomach upset, loose stools, or a sulfur taste. Ironically, nausea is one of the symptoms the supplement is supposed to help, so if it makes your stomach worse, stop.

**Who should be cautious or check with a doctor first:**

- **People with kidney disease or a history of kidney stones.** In particular, people with a genetic condition called **cystinuria** form stones made of cystine, and extra cysteine is not a good idea.
- **People with asthma**, mainly a concern with NAC, which in some forms can trigger airway spasms.
- **People taking nitroglycerin** or other nitrates for heart conditions. NAC is known to boost their effect and can cause headaches and low blood pressure. Whether plain L-cysteine does the same is less clear, so check with a pharmacist.
- **People on blood thinners or with bleeding disorders**, because NAC may have mild effects on clotting.
- **Pregnant or breastfeeding people**, since supplement doses haven't been studied for safety in pregnancy.
- **People with diabetes**, since some sulfur amino acids may affect blood sugar handling. Ask your doctor before adding them.

**Quality matters.** In the US, dietary supplements aren't approved by the FDA before they're sold, and the amount on the label isn't always what's in the bottle. Look for products tested by an independent group such as USP or NSF when you can.

### What L-cysteine can't do

It's worth being blunt here, because supplement marketing often isn't:

- **It doesn't lower your blood alcohol level** in any meaningful way and won't make you less impaired. Don't drive after drinking, whatever you've taken.
- **It doesn't protect your liver from heavy drinking.** There's no human evidence that taking cysteine offsets the liver damage caused by drinking too much over time.
- **It doesn't prevent alcohol poisoning.** If someone is confused, vomiting while barely conscious, breathing slowly, or can't be woken, call 911. No supplement changes that.
- **It won't fix a hangover from drinking far past your limit.** The Finnish study found reductions in some symptoms, not elimination of the hangover.

## Food Sources of Cysteine

You can get cysteine from a normal diet, and eating well around drinking is helpful for many reasons. Foods relatively rich in cysteine and its building block methionine include:

- Eggs
- Chicken and turkey
- Yogurt, cheese, and milk
- Beans and lentils
- Sunflower seeds and oats
- Garlic and onions, which contain other sulfur compounds

The doses used in the hangover trial were taken as concentrated tablets during drinking, so a meal isn't the same thing. But eating a protein-rich meal before you drink slows how quickly alcohol reaches your blood, which is one of the better-supported ways to reduce how rough you feel the next day. The old idea that eggs help a hangover may owe something to their cysteine content, though no one has tested eggs for that specifically.

## Where L-Cysteine Fits in a Hangover Plan

If you rank hangover strategies by how strong the evidence is, the list looks like this:

1. **Drink less, and drink slower.** This is the only approach that reliably prevents hangovers. The amount you drink is the biggest factor by far.
2. **Eat before and while drinking, and alternate with water.** Food slows absorption; water helps with thirst and dry mouth, even though dehydration isn't the whole story.
3. **Protect your sleep.** A lot of hangover misery is just a bad night's sleep. Stop drinking a few hours before bed if you can.
4. **Choose lower-congener drinks.** Clear spirits tend to cause milder hangovers than dark spirits for the same amount of alcohol.
5. **Supplements with some human data,** such as L-cysteine, come after all of the above. They might take the edge off. They can't undo heavy drinking.

Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) goes through these habits in order, and our planned guide on [what to take before drinking](/never-hungover/what-to-take-before-drinking) compares the pre-drinking options side by side.

### L-cysteine and "hangxiety"

The 600 mg result on stress and anxiety caught a lot of attention, because next-day anxiety is one of the most unpleasant parts of a hangover for many people. It's an intriguing finding, but it came from a small number of people at one dose level, so treat it as a lead rather than an answer. If hangover anxiety is your main problem, our [hangxiety guide](/never-hungover/hangxiety-complete-guide-2026-supplements-research) covers why it happens and what else may help. If you regularly feel anxious or low after drinking, that's worth raising with a doctor, as it can be a sign that alcohol is affecting your mood more than you'd like.

## Our Verdict

L-cysteine has more human hangover evidence than most of the ingredients on the supplement shelf, which is a low bar but a real one. The 2020 Finnish trial is well designed for its size, and its results for nausea and headache at 1,200 mg are a reasonable basis for curiosity. But it's one small study in young men, using a tablet that included vitamins, and it hasn't been independently repeated. Its closest relative, NAC, didn't show a clear overall benefit in its own small trial.

If you'd like to try L-cysteine, take it during drinking rather than after, stay around the studied amount, take it with food, and skip it if you have kidney problems or take medicines that might interact. And keep your expectations honest. It may make a rough morning a little less rough. Drinking less will do much more.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Does L-cysteine actually work for hangovers?**

There's some evidence it may help. A 2020 randomized, placebo-controlled trial from Finland, published in *Alcohol and Alcoholism*, found that 1,200 mg of L-cysteine taken during heavy drinking reduced next-day nausea and headache, and a 600 mg dose was linked to less stress and anxiety. But the study had only 19 young men, the tablet also contained vitamins, and no independent team has repeated it yet. Treat it as promising, not proven.

**How much L-cysteine should I take for a hangover?**

There's no official dose. The only human hangover study used 1,200 mg in total, split across the drinking session, with 600 mg also tested. There's no evidence that taking more helps more. If your hangover product already contains L-cysteine, count that toward the total, and check with a doctor first if you have kidney problems or take regular medication.

**When should I take L-cysteine, before or after drinking?**

In the study that showed a benefit, L-cysteine was taken during the drinking session, not the next morning. The idea is that it needs to be in your system while your liver is producing acetaldehyde. Taking it only once you already feel hungover hasn't been tested and may do little.

**What's the difference between L-cysteine and NAC for hangovers?**

NAC (N-acetylcysteine) is cysteine with a small acetyl group attached, and the body converts it back to cysteine. NAC is more stable and is used in hospitals as the antidote for acetaminophen overdose. For hangovers specifically, plain L-cysteine has the more encouraging trial so far, while a small 2021 NAC trial found no clear overall benefit, with a possible effect in women that needs confirming.

**Is L-cysteine safe to take with alcohol?**

For most healthy adults, L-cysteine at the amounts used in hangover research appears to be well tolerated, with stomach upset the most common side effect. It doesn't reduce your blood alcohol level, doesn't make you less impaired, and doesn't protect your liver from heavy drinking. People with kidney disease, a history of kidney stones or cystinuria, pregnancy, or those taking nitrates or blood thinners should talk to a doctor first.

**Can I take L-cysteine with DHM?**

There's no known harmful interaction, and some hangover products combine the two. They're thought to work in different ways: cysteine targets acetaldehyde and glutathione, while DHM has been studied mainly in animals for effects on alcohol metabolism and the brain. Neither has large human trials for hangovers, so the combination is reasonable to try but not proven to beat either one alone.

**Does L-cysteine help with hangover anxiety?**

In the 2020 Finnish trial, the 600 mg dose was linked to lower next-day stress and anxiety. That's an interesting result, but it came from a small group at a single dose and hasn't been repeated. If you often feel anxious after drinking, cutting back on alcohol and protecting your sleep are more reliable, and persistent anxiety is worth discussing with a doctor.

**Can I get enough cysteine from food instead?**

Eggs, poultry, dairy, beans, oats, and seeds all provide cysteine or the building blocks your body uses to make it, and a protein-rich meal before drinking is a good idea for other reasons. But the hangover study used concentrated tablets taken during drinking, so a normal meal isn't an equivalent dose. Food alone hasn't been tested as a hangover treatment in this way.
